subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Debt Snowball vs. Avalanche
description: Learn The Debt Snowball vs. Avalanche in one minute.

hook.text: Math says pay the highest-interest debt first. Psychology says pay the smallest balance. Which wins?

buildup.text: The avalanche method minimizes interest paid. The snowball method — paying smallest debts first — provides quick wins.

discovery.text: Gal and McShane found that people using the snowball method paid off debt faster in real life.

twist.text: The 'best' strategy is the one you follow through on. A perfect plan abandoned is worse than an imperfect plan.

climax.text: If you need motivation, go snowball. If you're already disciplined, go avalanche. Know your psychology, not your math.

punchline.text: The best debt plan is the one you finish.

quiz.question: Why does the snowball method often outperform the avalanche in practice?
options: It always saves the most money
Quick wins from paying off small debts sustain motivation

details.summary: The debt avalanche method pays highest-interest debt first to minimize total cost, while the debt snowball method pays smallest balances first for quick psychological wins. The snowball method is mathematically worse but psychologically more effective for most people.
details.whyItMatters: The debt snowball versus avalanche debate perfectly illustrates the tension between economic rationality and behavioral effectiveness.
takeaways: The avalanche method minimizes total interest paid but lacks early wins
The snowball method provides motivating quick victories that sustain effort
Research shows snowball users are more likely to eliminate all their debt

faq.question: Why do behavioral economists prefer the snowball method?
faq.answer: Eliminating a small debt entirely provides a powerful sense of accomplishment. This psychological win motivates continued effort. The avalanche method shows slow progress on large debts for months, which discourages many people into abandoning the plan entirely.

faq.question: When is the avalanche method actually better?
faq.answer: When interest rate differences are large and the person has strong financial discipline. If your highest-rate debt is also relatively small, both methods converge anyway. The key is honestly assessing whether you need motivational wins to stay on track.
